Title: Tips for debugging .htaccess rewrite rules. Body:

Many posters have problems debugging their RewriteRule and RewriteCond statements within their .htaccess files. Most of these are using a shared hosting service and therefore don't have access to the root server configuration. They cannot avoid using .htaccess files for rewriting and cannot enable a RewriteLogLevel" as many respondents suggest. Also there are many .htaccess-specific pitfalls and constraints are aren't covered well. Setting up a local test LAMP stack involves too much of a learning curve for most.

So my Q here is how would we recommend that they debug their rules themselves. I provide a few suggestions below. Other suggestions would be appreciated.

  1. Understand that the mod_rewrite engine cycles through .htaccess files. The engine runs this loop:

    do
  execute server and vhost rewrites (in the Apache Virtual Host Config)
  find the lowest "Per Dir" .htaccess file on the file path with rewrites enabled
  if found(.htaccess)
     execute .htaccess rewrites (in the user's directory)
while rewrite occurred

    So your rules will get executed repeatedly and if you change the URI path then it may end up executing other .htaccessfiles if they exist. So make sure that you terminate this loop, if necessary by adding extra RewriteCond to stop rules firing. Also delete any lower level .htaccess rewrite rulesets unless explicitly intent to use multi-level rulesets.

  2. Make sure that the syntax of each Regexp is correct by testing against a set of test patterns to make sure that is a valid syntax and does what you intend with a fully range of test URIs. See answer below for more details.

  3. Build up your rules incrementally in a test directory. You can make use of the "execute the deepest .htaccess file on the path feature" to set up a separate test directory (tree) and debug rulesets here without screwing up your main rules and stopping your site working. You have to add them one at a time because this is the only way to localise failures to individual rules.

  4. Use a dummy script stub to dump out server and environment variables. (See Listing 2)If your app uses, say, blog/index.php then you can copy this into test/blog/index.php and use it to test out your blog rules in the test subdirectory. You can also use environment variables to make sure that the rewrite engine in interpreting substitution strings correctly, e.g.

    RewriteRule ^(.*) - [E=TEST0:%{DOCUMENT_ROOT}/blog/html_cache/$1.html]

    and look for these REDIRECT_* variables in the phpinfo dump. BTW, I used this one and discovered on my site that I had to use %{ENV:DOCUMENT_ROOT_REAL} instead. In the case of redirector looping REDIRECT_REDIRECT_* variables list the previous pass. Etc..

  5. Make sure that you don't get bitten by your browser caching incorrect 301 redirects. See answer below. My thanks to Ulrich Palha for this.

  6. The rewrite engine seems sensitive to cascaded rules within an .htaccess context, (that is where a RewriteRule results in a substitution and this falls though to further rules), as I found bugs with internal sub-requests (1), and incorrect PATH_INFO processing which can often be prevents by use of the [NS], [L] and [PT] flags.

Any more comment or suggestions?

Listing 1 -- phpinfo

<?php phpinfo(INFO_ENVIRONMENT|INFO_VARIABLES);
answer:
```python
def debug_htaccess_rules():
    """
    This function provides tips for debugging .htaccess rewrite rules on shared hosting services.
    
    It explains common pitfalls and constraints, suggests best practices, and includes examples of how to debug rules manually.
    """
    # Step 1: Understand the mod_rewrite cycle
    print("Understanding the mod_rewrite cycle:")
    print("The engine executes the following steps repeatedly:")
    print("1. Execute server and vhost rewrites.")
    print("2. Find the lowest 'Per Dir' .htaccess file on the file path with rewrites enabled.")
    print("3. Execute .htaccess rewrites (in the user's directory).")
    print("Repeat until rewrite occurred.")

    # Step 2: Ensure valid Regexp syntax
    print("\nEnsure valid Regexp syntax:")
    print("Test against a set of test patterns to verify the correctness of each rule.")

    # Step 3: Build rules incrementally in a test directory
    print("\nBuild rules incrementally in a test directory:")
    print("Create a separate test directory and debug rules one at a time.")

    # Step 4: Use a dummy script stub to dump environment variables
    print("\nUse a dummy script stub to dump environment variables:")
    print("Copy a PHP script into the test directory and run it to view server and environment variables.")
    print("Check REDIRECT_* variables for redirection information.")

    # Step 5: Be aware of browser caching incorrect 301 redirects
    print("\nBe aware of browser caching incorrect 301 redirects:")
    print("Test with different browsers and clear cache to ensure the issue persists.")

    # Step 6: Handle cascaded rules and PATH_INFO processing
    print("\nHandle cascaded rules and PATH_INFO processing:")
    print("Use the [N], [L], and [PT] flags to manage rule execution flow.")
    print("Avoid using internal sub-requests to prevent issues like loop detection.")

# Example usage
debug_htaccess_rules()
```

This Python function `debug_htaccess_rules` provides a comprehensive guide to debugging .htaccess rewrite rules on shared hosting services. It covers understanding the mod_rewrite cycle, ensuring valid Regexp syntax, building rules incrementally, using a dummy script stub to dump environment variables, being aware of browser caching, handling cascaded rules, and managing PATH_INFO processing.

Title: Save PL/pgSQL output from PostgreSQL to a CSV file. Body:

What is the easiest way to save PL/pgSQL output from a PostgreSQL database to a CSV file?

I'm using PostgreSQL 8.4 with pgAdmin III and PSQL plugin where I run queries from.
answer:
To save PL/pgSQL output from a PostgreSQL database to a CSV file, you can use the following Python code snippet. This example assumes you have a function named `my_plpgsql_function` that returns data that needs to be exported to a CSV file.

```python
import psycopg2
import csv

# Connect to your PostgreSQL database
conn = psycopg2.connect(
    dbname="your_database",
    user="your_username",
    password="your_password",
    host="your_host"
)

# Create a cursor object
cur = conn.cursor()

# Execute the PL/pgSQL function
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM my_plpgsql_function()")

# Fetch all rows from the result set
rows = cur.fetchall()

# Open a CSV file for writing
with open('output.csv', mode='w', newline='') as file:
    writer = csv.writer(file)
    
    # Write the header row (assuming the function returns columns)
    headers = [desc[0] for desc in cur.description]
    writer.writerow(headers)
    
    # Write each row of data to the CSV file
    for row in rows:
        writer.writerow(row)

# Close the cursor and connection
cur.close()
conn.close()

print("PL/pgSQL output has been saved to output.csv")
```

### Explanation:

1. **Database Connection**: The code connects to the PostgreSQL database using `psycopg2`. Replace `"your_database"`, `"your_username"`, `"your_password"`, and `"your_host"` with your actual database credentials and hostname.

2. **Cursor Object**: A cursor object is created to execute SQL commands.

3. **Executing PL/pgSQL Function**: The `execute` method is used to call the PL/pgSQL function `my_plpgsql_function()` which should return the desired data.

4. **Fetching Data**: The `fetchall` method retrieves all rows of data returned by the query.

5. **Writing to CSV File**:
   - A CSV file named `output.csv` is opened in write mode.
   - A `csv.writer` object is created to handle the CSV operations.
   - The column names from the query description are extracted and written as the first row of the CSV file.
   - Each row of data fetched from the database is written to the CSV file.

6. **Closing Resources**: Finally, the cursor and connection are closed to free up resources.

This approach allows you to easily export the output of any PL/pgSQL function to a CSV file using Python.

```python
def import_csv_to_postgres(csv_file_path, table_name):
    # Connect to the PostgreSQL database

        dbname="your_database",
        user="your_username",
        password="your_password",
        host="localhost"
    )

    # Open the CSV file for reading

        csvreader = csv.reader(csvfile)
        
        # Initialize an empty list to store the data rows
        data_rows = []
        
        # Iterate over each row in the CSV file
        for row in csvreader:
            # Append the row data to the list
            data_rows.append(row)
    
    # Prepare the SQL query to insert data into the table
    insert_query = f"INSERT INTO {table_name} (column1, column2, column3) VALUES %s"
    
    # Execute the SQL query using the data rows
    execute_values(cur, insert_query, data_rows)
    
    # Commit the changes to the database
    conn.commit()
    
    # Close the cursor and connection
    cur.close()
    conn.close()
```

Title: What's the difference between faking, mocking, and stubbing?. Body:

I know how I use these terms, but I'm wondering if there are accepted definitions for faking, mocking, and stubbing for unit tests? How do you define these for your tests? Describe situations where you might use each.

Here is how I use them:

Fake: a class that implements an interface but contains fixed data and no logic. Simply returns "good" or "bad" data depending on the implementation.

Mock: a class that implements an interface and allows the ability to dynamically set the values to return/exceptions to throw from particular methods and provides the ability to check if particular methods have been called/not called.

Stub: Like a mock class, except that it doesn't provide the ability to verify that methods have been called/not called.

Generation of each:

  • Mocks and Stubs can be hand-generated or generated by a mocking framework.
  • Fake classes are generated by hand.

Using them as follows:

  • Mocks primarily to verify interactions between my class and dependent classes.
  • Stubs once I have verified the interactions and am testing alternate paths through my code.
  • Fake classes primarily to abstract out data dependencies or when mocks/stubs are too tedious to set up each time.

Title: How should I unit test multithreaded code?. Body:

I have thus far avoided the nightmare that is testing multi-threaded code since it just seems like too much of a minefield. I'd like to ask how people have gone about testing code that relies on threads for successful execution, or just how people have gone about testing those kinds of issues that only show up when two threads interact in a given manner?

This seems like a really key problem for programmers today, it would be useful to pool our knowledge on this one imho.
answer:
To unit test multithreaded code effectively, you can follow these steps:

1. **Isolate Threads**: Ensure that each thread has its own isolated environment. This can be achieved by using a mock object for any dependencies that the thread might rely on.

2. **Use Thread-Safe Data Structures**: Use data structures that are inherently thread-safe, such as `threading.Lock` or `queue.Queue`, which provide mechanisms for synchronizing access to shared resources.

3. **Mock Dependencies**: When testing, mock out any external dependencies that the threads depend on. This includes database connections, network calls, and other services that might not be available in your test environment.

4. **Test Threading Interactions**: Write tests that simulate interactions between different threads. For example, test that threads communicate correctly through shared variables or queues.

5. **Check Thread Safety**: Verify that all operations performed by threads do not lead to race conditions or deadlocks. You can use tools like `pytest-asyncio` to run asynchronous tests with asyncio.

6. **Concurrency Testing Frameworks**: Utilize frameworks designed specifically for concurrency testing, such as `concurrent.futures` from the standard library or third-party libraries like `pytest-concurrent`.

7. **Thread Pooling**: Consider using a thread pool to manage multiple threads efficiently. This helps in reducing overhead and makes the test suite more scalable.

Here's an example of how you might set up a basic test case for multithreaded code using Python's `unittest` framework and `threading` module:

```python
import threading
import unittest

# Mock dependency
class Database:
    def query(self, sql):
        return "Result"

# Thread class
class QueryThread(threading.Thread):
    def __init__(self, db, sql):
        super().__init__()
        self.db = db
        self.sql = sql

    def run(self):
        result = self.db.query(self.sql)
        print(f"Query result: {result}")

class TestQueryThread(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.db = Database()
        self.sql = "SELECT * FROM users"

    def test_query_thread(self):
        # Create and start multiple threads
        threads = []
        for _ in range(5):
            thread = QueryThread(self.db, self.sql)
            threads.append(thread)
            thread.start()

        # Wait for all threads to complete
        for thread in threads:
            thread.join()

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
```

In this example, we create a `Database` class that simulates a database interaction. We then define a `QueryThread` class that inherits from `threading.Thread`. The `run` method of `QueryThread` executes a query against the database using the mocked `Database` instance.

In the `TestQueryThread` class, we set up the `Database` instance and the SQL query. We then create multiple instances of `QueryThread`, start them, and wait for them to complete. This ensures that the threads execute concurrently and that the results are as expected.

By following these steps and using appropriate tools, you can effectively test multithreaded code in your Python projects.

Title: Difference between @Mock and @InjectMocks. Body:

What is the difference between @Mock and @InjectMocks in Mockito framework?
answer:
```python
# Importing the necessary module from Mockito
from mock import Mock, patch

# Defining a function to demonstrate the difference between @Mock and @InjectMocks
def explain_mock_injectmocks():
    # Using the @patch decorator to mock the class being tested
    with patch('module.ClassToTest') as ClassToTest:
        # Creating an instance of Mock for the mocked class
        mock_class = ClassToTest()
        
        # Assuming ClassToTest has a method called 'some_method'
        # We can use mock_class.some_method() to call the method and return a value
        result = mock_class.some_method()
        print(f"Method returned: {result}")

        # Using @InjectMocks annotation to inject mocks into the class under test
        class_to_test = ClassToTest(mock_class)
        
        # Now we can call the same method on the injected mock object
        result_from_injection = class_to_test.some_method()
        print(f"Method returned (injected): {result_from_injection}")
        
        # The first method call should be to the mocked version
        assert result != result_from_injection, "The methods did not return different results."

# Call the function to demonstrate the difference
explain_mock_injectmocks()
```

In this solution, we use the `@patch` decorator to mock the class `ClassToTest`. This allows us to isolate the class under test from its dependencies and focus on testing its behavior without needing real instances of those dependencies.

Next, we create an instance of `Mock` for `ClassToTest` and use it to call a method named `some_method`. We then demonstrate how to use the `@InjectMocks` annotation to inject this mocked object into another class `class_to_test`. By calling `class_to_test.some_method()` again, we see that the method now returns a different result, indicating that the mocking was successful.

Finally, we perform an assertion to ensure that the methods returned different results. This demonstrates the key difference between using `@Mock` to mock classes and using `@InjectMocks` to inject them into other classes, allowing for more flexible and maintainable unit tests.

Title: How to save/restore a model after training?. Body:

After you train a model in Tensorflow:

  1. How do you save the trained model?
  2. How do you later restore this saved model?
answer:
To save and restore a TensorFlow model after training, you can follow these steps:

1. **Save the Model**: Use the `tf.keras.models.save_model` function to save the entire model including its architecture, weights, and optimizer state.

```python
# Importing necessary libraries
import tensorflow as tf

# Assuming you have a trained model named 'model'
model = tf.keras.models.load_model('path_to_your_saved_model.h5')
```

2. **Restore the Model**: After saving the model, you can load it back into memory using the `tf.keras.models.load_model` function with the same path or file name.

```python
# Restoring the model from disk
restored_model = tf.keras.models.load_model('path_to_your_saved_model.h5')
```

Here's a complete example of how to save and restore a model:

```python
# Example model creation (for demonstration purposes)
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu', input_shape=(784,)),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')
])

# Compile the model
model.compile(optimizer='adam',
              loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
              metrics=['accuracy'])

# Simulate training (this step would involve actual data loading and model fitting)
# For demonstration, we'll just create some dummy data
dummy_data = tf.random.normal((100, 784))
dummy_labels = tf.random.uniform((100,), minval=0, maxval=9, dtype=tf.int32)

model.fit(dummy_data, dummy_labels, epochs=5)

# Save the model
model.save('my_model.h5')

# Later restore the model
restored_model = tf.keras.models.load_model('my_model.h5')

# Evaluate the restored model
test_loss, test_acc = restored_model.evaluate(dummy_data, dummy_labels)
print(f"Test accuracy: {test_acc}")
```

In this example:
- The model is first compiled and trained on some dummy data.
- The trained model is then saved using `model.save('my_model.h5')`.
- Later, the model is loaded from the saved file using `tf.keras.models.load_model('my_model.h5')`.
- Finally, the restored model is evaluated on the same dummy dataset to confirm that it performs well.

This approach allows you to easily save and restore models for further use or sharing.

Title: What is the difference between 'SAME' and 'VALID' padding in tf.nn.max_pool of tensorflow?. Body:

What is the difference between 'SAME' and 'VALID' padding in tf.nn.max_pool of tensorflow?

In my opinion, 'VALID' means there will be no zero padding outside the edges when we do max pool.

According to A guide to convolution arithmetic for deep learning, it says that there will be no padding in pool operator, i.e. just use 'VALID' of tensorflow. But what is 'SAME' padding of max pool in tensorflow?
answer:
To understand the difference between 'SAME' and 'VALID' padding in `tf.nn.max_pool` in TensorFlow, let's break down each concept:

### Same Padding

In TensorFlow, 'SAME' padding ensures that the output size of the pooling operation is the same as the input size. This means that if you apply a pooling layer with 'SAME' padding to an image of size `(height, width, channels)`, the output size will also be `(height, width, channels)`.

#### Why Same Padding?

- **Preservation of Spatial Dimensions**: By using 'SAME' padding, the output dimensions match those of the input, preserving the spatial information. This is particularly useful when you want to ensure that the output features capture relevant spatial patterns.
  
- **Efficient Padding**: Since 'SAME' padding does not introduce any extra zero-padding at the edges of the input, it can lead to more efficient computation, especially for large inputs or deeper networks.

### Valid Padding

In contrast, 'VALID' padding removes all the padding from the edges of the input tensor before applying the pooling operation. This means that the output size of the pooling operation will be smaller than the input size by half (for 2D operations).

#### Why Valid Padding?

- **Efficiency**: Removing padding allows for faster computations because there is no need to handle extra padding values during the forward pass.
  
- **Reduced Output Size**: The output size is reduced, which might be beneficial for reducing memory usage or computational complexity, especially for large datasets or deeper neural networks.

### Example Usage

Here’s how you can use 'SAME' and 'VALID' padding in TensorFlow:

```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Define the input tensor
input_tensor = tf.constant([[[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]]]],
                         dtype=tf.float32)

# Apply SAME padding
same_padded_output = tf.nn.max_pool(input_tensor, ksize=[1, 2, 2, 1], strides=[1, 2, 2, 1], padding='SAME')
print("Same Padding Output:\n", same_padded_output.numpy())

# Apply VALID padding
valid_padded_output = tf.nn.max_pool(input_tensor, ksize=[1, 2, 2, 1], strides=[1, 2, 2, 1], padding='VALID')
print("Valid Padding Output:\n", valid_padded_output.numpy())
```

### Explanation

- **Same Padding**:
  - Input shape: `(1, 2, 2, 1)`
  - Output shape: `(1, 2, 2, 1)`

- **Valid Padding**:
  - Input shape: `(1, 2, 2, 1)`
  - Output shape: `(1, 1, 1, 1)`

By understanding the differences between 'SAME' and 'VALID' padding, you can choose the appropriate method based on your specific requirements for handling padding and output size.

Title: How to prevent tensorflow from allocating the totality of a GPU memory?. Body:

I work in an environment in which computational resources are shared, i.e., we have a few server machines equipped with a few Nvidia Titan X GPUs each.

For small to moderate size models, the 12 GB of the Titan X is usually enough for 2–3 people to run training concurrently on the same GPU. If the models are small enough that a single model does not take full advantage of all the computational units of the GPU, this can actually result in a speedup compared with running one training process after the other. Even in cases where the concurrent access to the GPU does slow down the individual training time, it is still nice to have the flexibility of having multiple users simultaneously train on the GPU.

The problem with TensorFlow is that, by default, it allocates the full amount of available GPU memory when it is launched. Even for a small two-layer neural network, I see that all 12 GB of the GPU memory is used up.

Is there a way to make TensorFlow only allocate, say, 4 GB of GPU memory, if one knows that this is enough for a given model?
answer:
To prevent TensorFlow from allocating the total of a GPU memory, you can use the `gpus` parameter in the `tf.config.experimental.list_physical_devices('GPU')` function. This allows you to specify the number of GPUs that TensorFlow should use.

Here's an example code snippet:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# List physical devices (including GPUs)
physical_devices = tf.config.experimental.list_physical_devices('GPU')

# Check if there are any GPUs available
if len(physical_devices) > 0:
    # Set the number of GPUs to be used
    gpus = [physical_devices[0]]  # For example, using only the first GPU
    try:
        # Restrict TensorFlow to only use the specified GPUs
        tf.config.experimental.set_visible_devices(gpus, 'GPU')
        print("TensorFlow has been configured to use only", len(gpus), "GPU(s).")
    except RuntimeError as e:
        # If a GPU is already in use, TensorFlow will raise a RuntimeError
        print(e)
else:
    print("No GPUs found.")
```
In this code, we first list all the physical devices (including GPUs) using `tf.config.experimental.list_physical_devices('GPU')`. We then check if there are any GPUs available. If there are, we set the number of GPUs to be used to one (in this case, the first GPU). Finally, we use `tf.config.experimental.set_visible_devices()` to restrict TensorFlow to only use the specified GPUs.

tf.variable_op_scope(values, name, default_name, initializer=None)

Returns a context manager for defining an op that creates variables. This context manager validates that the given values are from the same graph, ensures that that graph is the default graph, and pushes a name scope and a variable scope.

tf.op_scope(values, name, default_name=None)

Returns a context manager for use when defining a Python op. This context manager validates that the given values are from the same graph, ensures that that graph is the default graph, and pushes a name scope.

tf.name_scope(name)

Wrapper for Graph.name_scope() using the default graph. See Graph.name_scope() for more details.

tf.variable_scope(name_or_scope, reuse=None, initializer=None)

What's the best cross-platform way to get file creation and modification dates/times, that works on both Linux and Windows?
answer:
To retrieve file creation and modification dates/times across different operating systems like Linux and Windows, you can use the `os` module in Python which provides a portable way of using operating system dependent functionality.

Here's how you can implement this:

```python
import os

def get_file_dates(file_path):
    """
    Get the creation and modification dates of a file.

    Args:
    file_path (str): The path to the file.

    Returns:
    tuple: A tuple containing two elements, the first being the creation date and time,
           and the second being the modification date and time.
    """
    # Get the creation time and modification time
```

3. **Getting File Creation and Modification Times**:
   - `os.path.getctime(file_path)`: This function returns the time of last access to the specified file as a floating-point number of seconds since the epoch (January 1, 1970).
   - `os.path.getmtime(file_path)`: This function returns the time of last modification to the specified file as a floating-point number of seconds since the epoch.

Title: Class (static) variables and methods. Body:

How do I create class (i.e. static) variables or methods in Python?
answer:
```python
class MyClass:
    # Static variable shared by all instances of MyClass
    static_var = 0

    def __init__(self):
        # Instance variable unique to each instance of MyClass
        self.instance_var = 0

    @staticmethod
    def static_method():
        # Accessing static variable
        print("Accessing static variable:", MyClass.static_var)
        # Modifying static variable
        MyClass.static_var += 1

    def instance_method(self):
        # Accessing instance variable
        print("Accessing instance variable:", self.instance_var)
        # Modifying instance variable
        self.instance_var += 1

# Create instances of MyClass
obj1 = MyClass()
obj2 = MyClass()

# Call static method on the class itself
MyClass.static_method()

# Call instance method on each object
obj1.instance_method()
obj2.instance_method()

# Print final values of static and instance variables
print("Final value of static variable:", MyClass.static_var)
print("Final value of instance variable for obj1:", obj1.instance_var)
print("Final value of instance variable for obj2:", obj2.instance_var)
```

This Python code defines a class `MyClass` with two types of variables and methods:

1. **Static Variables**: These are defined within the class but outside any method. They are accessed using the class name rather than an instance of the class. In this example, `static_var` is a static variable that can be accessed directly from the class without needing to instantiate it.

2. **Instance Variables**: These are defined within the constructor (`__init__`) of the class and are specific to each instance of the class. They are accessed using the instance name.

3. **Static Methods**: These are defined with the `@staticmethod` decorator and can access either static variables or instance variables through the class name. They cannot modify instance variables directly; instead, they should use parameters to update them if needed.

The code creates instances of `MyClass`, calls both static and instance methods, and prints out the final values of the static and instance variables to demonstrate their behavior.

What is the difference between old style and new style classes in Python? When should I use one or the other?
answer:
```python
class OldStyleClass:
    def __init__(self):
        self.value = "This is an old-style class."

    def display(self):
        print("Old-style class value:", self.value)

class NewStyleClass(object):

new_instance.display()  # Output: New-style class value: This is a new-style class.

```

In this solution, we define two classes: `OldStyleClass` and `NewStyleClass`. The main differences between these classes lie in how they interact with the built-in types and methods of Python. 

- **Old Style Class**: These classes do not inherit from any parent class other than `object`, which means they have no metaclass and cannot be used with the `isinstance()` function to check their type against `object`. They also do not support some advanced features like multiple inheritance and the `__slots__` attribute. 

- **New Style Class**: These classes inherit from `object`, which allows them to utilize features like multiple inheritance (`class A(object), class B(A)`) and the `__slots__` attribute for memory efficiency. Additionally, new style classes can use modern features introduced by Python 2.3, such as dictionary subclasses (`dict.__getitem__`, `dict.__setitem__`, `dict.__delitem__`). 

When deciding whether to use an old-style class or a new-style class, consider the following factors:

1. **Use of `object` as the base class**: If your class does not need to use features specific to new-style classes (like multiple inheritance or the `__slots__` attribute), using `object` as the base class will save you from writing boilerplate code and potentially improve performance.

2. **Compatibility with Python 2.3**: If your project requires compatibility with Python 2.3, it's recommended to use new-style classes due to their improved features and better support for the language's evolution.

3. **Modern features**: If your class uses features that are available in newer versions of Python, such as multiple inheritance, the use of new-style classes can provide more flexibility and functionality.

In summary, while both old-style and new-style classes exist in Python, new-style classes offer better compatibility with Python's latest features and are generally preferred for new projects.

Title: How can I pair socks from a pile efficiently?. Body:

Yesterday I was pairing the socks from the clean laundry and figured out the way I was doing it is not very efficient. I was doing a naive search — picking one sock and "iterating" the pile in order to find its pair. This requires iterating over n/2 * n/4 = n2/8 socks on average.

As a computer scientist I was thinking what I could do? Sorting (according to size/color/...) of course came to mind to achieve an O(NlogN) solution.

Hashing or other not-in-place solutions are not an option, because I am not able to duplicate my socks (though it could be nice if I could).

So, the question is basically:

Given a pile of n pairs of socks, containing 2n elements (assume each sock has exactly one matching pair), what is the best way to pair them up efficiently with up to logarithmic extra space? (I believe I can remember that amount of info if needed.)

I will appreciate an answer that addresses the following aspects:

  • A general theoretical solution for a huge number of socks.
  • The actual number of socks is not that large, I don't believe my spouse and I have more than 30 pairs. (And it is fairly easy to distinguish between my socks and hers; can this be used as well?)
  • Is it equivalent to the element distinctness problem?
answer:
To pair socks from a pile efficiently, we can use a hash map to keep track of the count of each color or type of sock. Here's how you can implement this in Python:

```python
def pair_socks(socks):
    # Initialize a dictionary to store the count of each sock
    sock_count = {}
    
    # Count the occurrences of each sock
    for sock in socks:
        if sock in sock_count:
            sock_count[sock] += 1
        else:
            sock_count[sock] = 1
    
    # Pair the socks
    paired_socks = []
    for sock, count in sock_count.items():
        if count % 2 == 0:
            # If the count is even, pair two socks
            paired_socks.append((sock, sock))
        elif count > 1:
            # If the count is odd, pair one sock and take one sock without a pair
            paired_socks.append((sock, sock))
    
    return paired_socks

# Example usage
socks = ['black', 'white', 'black', 'red', 'white', 'red']
paired_socks = pair_socks(socks)
print(paired_socks)  # Output: [('black', 'black'), ('white', 'white'), ('red', 'red')]
```

### Explanation:
1. **Initialization**: We initialize an empty dictionary `sock_count` to store the count of each sock.
2. **Counting**: We iterate through the list of socks and update the count in the dictionary. If the sock is already in the dictionary, we increment its count; otherwise, we add it to the dictionary with a count of 1.
3. **Pairing**: We iterate through the dictionary. For each sock, if its count is even, we pair it with another sock of the same color. If the count is odd, we pair one sock with itself and take one sock without a pair.
4. **Return**: Finally, we return the list of paired socks.

This approach ensures that we pair all socks in linear time (O(n)) and uses constant extra space (O(1)). The algorithm works efficiently even with up to 30 pairs of socks, making it suitable for most practical scenarios.

Title: Swift Beta performance: sorting arrays. Body:

I was implementing an algorithm in Swift Beta and noticed that the performance was very poor. After digging deeper I realized that one of the bottlenecks was something as simple as sorting arrays. The relevant part is here:

let n = 1000000
var x =  [Int](repeating: 0, count: n)
for i in 0..<n {
    x[i] = random()
}
// start clock here
let y = sort(x)
// stop clock here

In C++, a similar operation takes 0.06s on my computer.

In Python, it takes 0.6s (no tricks, just y = sorted(x) for a list of integers).

In Swift it takes 6s if I compile it with the following command:

xcrun swift -O3 -sdk `xcrun --show-sdk-path --sdk macosx`

And it takes as much as 88s if I compile it with the following command:

xcrun swift -O0 -sdk `xcrun --show-sdk-path --sdk macosx`

Timings in Xcode with "Release" vs. "Debug" builds are similar.

What is wrong here? I could understand some performance loss in comparison with C++, but not a 10-fold slowdown in comparison with pure Python.

Edit: weather noticed that changing -O3 to -Ofast makes this code run almost as fast as the C++ version! However, -Ofast changes the semantics of the language a lot — in my testing, it disabled the checks for integer overflows and array indexing overflows. For example, with -Ofast the following Swift code runs silently without crashing (and prints out some garbage):

let n = 10000000
print(n*n*n*n*n)
let x =  [Int](repeating: 10, count: n)
print(x[n])

So -Ofast is not what we want; the whole point of Swift is that we have the safety nets in place. Of course, the safety nets have some impact on the performance, but they should not make the programs 100 times slower. Remember that Java already checks for array bounds, and in typical cases, the slowdown is by a factor much less than 2. And in Clang and GCC we have got -ftrapv for checking (signed) integer overflows, and it is not that slow, either.

Hence the question: how can we get reasonable performance in Swift without losing the safety nets?

Edit 2: I did some more benchmarking, with very simple loops along the lines of

for i in 0..<n {
    x[i] = x[i] ^ 12345678
}

(Here the xor operation is there just so that I can more easily find the relevant loop in the assembly code. I tried to pick an operation that is easy to spot but also "harmless" in the sense that it should not require any checks related to integer overflows.)

Again, there was a huge difference in the performance between -O3 and -Ofast. So I had a look at the assembly code:

  • With -Ofast I get pretty much what I would expect. The relevant part is a loop with 5 machine language instructions.

  • With -O3 I get something that was beyond my wildest imagination. The inner loop spans 88 lines of assembly code. I did not try to understand all of it, but the most suspicious parts are 13 invocations of "callq _swift_retain" and another 13 invocations of "callq _swift_release". That is, 26 subroutine calls in the inner loop!

Edit 3: In comments, Ferruccio asked for benchmarks that are fair in the sense that they do not rely on built-in functions (e.g. sort). I think the following program is a fairly good example:

let n = 10000
var x = [Int](repeating: 1, count: n)
for i in 0..<n {
    for j in 0..<n {
        x[i] = x[j]
    }
}

There is no arithmetic, so we do not need to worry about integer overflows. The only thing that we do is just lots of array references. And the results are here—Swift -O3 loses by a factor almost 500 in comparison with -Ofast:

  • C++ -O3: 0.05 s
  • C++ -O0: 0.4 s
  • Java: 0.2 s
  • Python with PyPy: 0.5 s
  • Python: 12 s
  • Swift -Ofast: 0.05 s
  • Swift -O3: 23 s
  • Swift -O0: 443 s

(If you are concerned that the compiler might optimize out the pointless loops entirely, you can change it to e.g. x[i] ^= x[j], and add a print statement that outputs x[0]. This does not change anything; the timings will be very similar.)

And yes, here the Python implementation was a stupid pure Python implementation with a list of ints and nested for loops. It should be much slower than unoptimized Swift. Something seems to be seriously broken with Swift and array indexing.

Edit 4: These issues (as well as some other performance issues) seems to have been fixed in Xcode 6 beta 5.

For sorting, I now have the following timings:

  • clang++ -O3: 0.06 s
  • swiftc -Ofast: 0.1 s
  • swiftc -O: 0.1 s
  • swiftc: 4 s

For nested loops:

  • clang++ -O3: 0.06 s
  • swiftc -Ofast: 0.3 s
  • swiftc -O: 0.4 s
  • swiftc: 540 s

It seems that there is no reason anymore to use the unsafe -Ofast (a.k.a. -Ounchecked); plain -O produces equally good code.

```python
import time

def measure_time(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start_time = time.time()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        end_time = time.time()
        return result, end_time - start_time
    return wrapper

@measure_time
def sort_array(arr):
    return sorted(arr)

n = 1000000

print(f"Sorted array took {time_taken:.4f} seconds to generate.")
```

1. **Generate Short-Term Access Tokens**: These tokens should be short-lived (e.g., 5-10 minutes) and contain the user information needed for authentication.

2. **Use Long-Term Refresh Tokens**: These tokens should be longer-lived (e.g., 6 hours or more) and can be used to obtain new access tokens when the current one expires.

3. **Refresh Mechanism**: Implement a mechanism to refresh the access token when it expires. This can be done by sending a POST request to your server with the refresh token as a parameter.

4. **Token Storage**: Store both the short-term access token and the long-term refresh token securely. You might use a database or an in-memory cache depending on your requirements.

use admin

1) At the mongo command line, set the administrator:

    use admin;
    db.addUser('admin','123456');

2) Shutdown the server and exit

    db.shutdownServer();
    exit

3) Restart mongod with --auth

  $ sudo ./mongodb/bin/mongod --auth --dbpath /mnt/db/

4) Run mongo again in 2 ways:

   i) run mongo first then login:

        $ ./mongodb/bin/mongo localhost:27017
        use admin
        db.auth('admin','123456');

  ii) run & login to mongo in command line.

        $ ./mongodb/bin/mongo localhost:27017/admin -u admin -p 123456

The username & password will work the same way for mongodump and mongoexport.
